title: Cataract surgery: preparation, lens choices and recovery
intro: Cataract surgery removes the cloudy natural lens and replaces it with an artificial lens inside the eye. For many people it improves sight and daily activities, but the expected benefit depends on the rest of the eye as well as the cataract. Before consenting, discuss what matters to you, the proposed lens and anaesthetic, possible complications and the help you will need afterwards. The information here concerns adults.

sections.heading: Agree the aim and choose a lens
paragraphs: Measurements of the eye help select the artificial lens power. Explain whether reading, computer work or distance vision matters most. A monofocal lens focuses at a chosen distance, so glasses are commonly needed for other distances. Some alternative lenses offer a broader range but can involve trade-offs such as glare or halos and are not suitable for everyone. Ask how astigmatism, retinal disease or previous eye surgery affects the choice. No lens choice guarantees complete freedom from glasses or perfect vision.

sections.heading: Prepare with individual instructions
paragraphs: Bring a full list of medicines, allergies and previous eye procedures. Tell the team if you have trouble lying still, breathing flat, hearing instructions or applying drops. Follow the clinic's specific directions about contact lenses, eating, drinking and regular medicines: these vary with the planned anaesthetic and your health. Do not stop blood thinners or other prescriptions yourself. Arrange transport because you should not drive home, and plan support with drops or meals if needed. Ask for written instructions in a language you understand.

sections.heading: What happens during the operation
paragraphs: Most adult procedures use local anaesthesia, with the person awake, although another plan may be appropriate. The surgeon makes a small opening, removes the cloudy lens, often using ultrasound to break it up, and places the artificial lens in the remaining lens capsule. You may notice lights or movement; tell the team if you are uncomfortable. Many people go home the same day after checks. If both eyes need treatment, discuss the timing and plan for each eye with the surgeon rather than assuming a universal schedule.

sections.heading: Recovery and follow-up
paragraphs: Use the prescribed eye drops exactly as directed, keep follow-up appointments and follow the clinic's instructions about shields, washing and activity. Do not rub the eye. Vision may initially be blurry and improve over time; glasses may need updating after healing. Return to driving, lifting, sport and work depends on the eye's recovery and local requirements. Ask before restarting. Mild grittiness can occur, but worsening pain or vision should not simply be accepted as normal recovery.

sections.heading: Complications and warning signs
paragraphs: Possible complications include infection, inflammation, pressure changes, retinal detachment and problems with the lens or capsule; some require more treatment or surgery. Contact the eye service immediately for worsening sight, significant persistent pain, marked redness, new flashes or many new floaters, or a dark curtain across vision. Use urgent or emergency eye care if the surgical team cannot be reached. Later clouding can come from the capsule behind the implant rather than the original cataract growing back. This may be treatable with a laser after examination; do not diagnose the cause yourself.

examples.title: Choosing around everyday needs — hypothetical example
examples.text: A person reads for long periods and also drives at night. They ask how each lens choice affects reading glasses, distance vision and halos rather than assuming the most expensive option is best. The surgeon considers the health of the eye too.

examples.title: A change after going home — hypothetical example
examples.text: A person notices increasing pain and poorer vision after initially improving. They call the eye service immediately using the discharge contact rather than waiting for the routine follow-up. The team assesses the cause and treatment urgency.

questions: What improvement is realistic, and what are the trade-offs of the proposed lens?
What are my exact medicine, fasting, drop and transport instructions?
